name: E-democracy
summary: E-democracy (digital or internet democracy) holds that information and communication technology can deepen democratic life through online information, discussion, participation and sometimes direct or delegated voting. Its adherents mostly work within existing representative systems, aiming at more active citizen involvement, transparency and responsiveness, while treating security, privacy and the digital divide as serious risks. It is a procedural outlook and takes no side on most questions of economic or social policy.
scope: The mainstream civic-tech strand: Steven Clift's definition (coined 1994, Minnesota E-Democracy), participatory and deliberative platforms such as Decidim, and liquid-democracy tools like LiquidFeedback used by Pirate Parties. It excludes e-government service delivery as such and fringe technocratic or algorithmic-rule proposals. Most economic and social statements are answered neutral with low confidence because the ideology is procedural.

sources.usedFor: Definition: ICT used by democratic actors in political and governance processes at all levels, with greater and more direct citizen participation.

universal-healthcare.rationale: E-democracy is a method of political participation, not an economic program; adherents span the spectrum on health policy.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Nothing in e-democracy's doctrine addresses wage floors; it is a procedural stance and adherents differ.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The ideology is about civic technology and participation, not market versus state allocation, so adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: No source ties e-democracy to ownership of utilities; it is indifferent on the question.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Tax levels are not part of e-democracy's concerns; adherents hold varied views.

unions-good.rationale: Labor organization is outside the scope of e-democracy as documented; no position can be inferred.

property-fundamental.rationale: Property rights are not discussed in e-democracy sources; adherents are split.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation is not addressed by the ideology; its adherents are drawn from many economic camps.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare policy is outside e-democracy's procedural focus, so there is no inferable stance.

worker-ownership.rationale: Business ownership structures are not a theme of e-democracy; indifferent.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy is unrelated to e-democracy; adherents are split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Online deliberation advocates debate moderation, but the ideology takes no common line on legal speech limits.

strong-leader.rationale: E-democracy aims at more active citizen participation and revocable delegation, the opposite of a leader bypassing gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Its definition has governments and elected officials as legitimate democratic actors working with citizens; it seeks to improve governance, not abolish the state.

notes: E-democracy is a procedural family, so most substantive policy answers are neutral and low confidence and will not count as stated positions. Strands differ: liquid democracy leans to direct and delegated voting, while others only add consultation to representative institutions.
